'''''Prunus serrulata''''' or '''Japanese cherry'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a [[species]] of cherry tree that grows wild in [[Japan]], [[China]], [[Korea]] and [[Vietnam]]. The term also refers to a [[cultivar]] produced from ''[[Prunus speciosa]]'' (Oshima cherry), a cherry tree [[Endemism|endemic]] in Japan.<ref name ="Prunus">[http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=a915 Prunus serrulata]</ref><ref name ="katsuki2015137">Toshio Katsuki. (2015) ''Sakura''. p.137 [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref> Historically, the Japanese have developed many cultivars by selective breeding of cherry trees, which are produced by the complicated crossing of several wild species, and they are used for ornamental purposes all over the world. Of these, the cultivars produced by complex interspecific hybrids based on the Oshima cherry are also known as the '''''Cerasus'' Sato-zakura Group'''.<ref name ="katsuki2015137"/><ref name ="ojfc">{{cite web|title=Origins of Japanese flowering cherry (Prunus subgenus Cerasus) cultivars revealed using nuclear SSR markers|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260047309|work=Shuri Kato, Asako Matsumoto, Kensuke Yoshimura, Toshio Katsuki etc.|access-date=February 27, 2021}}</ref><ref name ="ojfcffrri">{{cite web|title=Origins of Japanese flowering cherry (Prunus subgenus Cerasus) cultivars revealed using nuclear SSR markers|url=https://www.ffpri.affrc.go.jp/research/saizensen/2014/20140616-01.html|work=Forestry and Forest Products Research Institute.|date=June 16, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190309150440/https://www.ffpri.affrc.go.jp/research/saizensen/2014/20140616-01.html|access-date=February 27, 2021|archive-date=2019-03-09}}</ref>

== Varieties and form ==
=== Classification ===
The classification of cherry blossoms varies from country to country and from period to period. For example, in the Japanese classification, ''P. serrulata'' Lindl. f. ''albida'', ''P. serrulata'' var. ''spontanea'', ''P. serrulata'' var. ''pubescens'' and ''P. serrulata'' Lindl. var. ''sachalinensis'', the  [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] and [[form (botany)|form]] constituting this [[species]], are classified as independent species because of their genetic, morphological, and flowering time differences.<ref name = "katsuki2015156">Toshio Katsuki (2015). ''Sakura'' pp.156-170. [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref>

There are several [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] and [[form (botany)|form]] (or species):
* '''''Prunus serrulata'' f. ''albida''''' (syn. '''''[[Prunus speciosa]]'''''). Japan.<ref name = "katsuki2015spe">Toshio Katsuki (2015). ''Sakura'' p.89. pp.166-170. [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref>
* '''''Prunus serrulata'' var. ''spontanea''''' or '''''Prunus serrulata'' f. ''spontanea''''' (syn. '''[[:ja:ヤマザクラ|''Prunus yamasakura'']]'''). Japan.<ref name = "katsuki2015jama">Toshio Katsuki (2015). ''Sakura'' pp.156-160. [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref>
:Some books say that ''P. yamasakura'' grows wild in China and Korea, but ''[[Prunus leveilleana|P. leveilleana]]'' and ''[[Prunus sargentii|P. sargentii]]'' were mistaken for ''P. yamasakura''.<ref name = "katsuki2015jama"/>
* '''''Prunus serrulata'' var. ''pubescens'''''  (syn. '''''[[Prunus leveilleana]]'''''). Japan, Korea, China.<ref name = "katsuki2015pub">Toshio Katsuki (2015). ''Sakura'' pp.160-163. [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref>
* '''''Prunus serrulata'' var. ''sachalinensis'''''  (syn. '''''[[Prunus sargentii]]'''''). Japan, Korea, eastern Russia, China.<ref name = "katsuki2015sar">Toshio Katsuki (2015). ''Sakura'' pp.163-166. [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref>

=== Trees and flowers ===
''Prunus serrulata'' is a small [[deciduous]] [[tree]] with a short single trunk, with a dense crown reaching a height of {{convert|26|-|39|ft|m|disp=flip}}. The smooth [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is chestnut-brown, with prominent horizontal [[lenticel]]s. The [[leaf|leaves]] are arranged alternately, simple, ovate-lanceolate, 5–13 cm long and 2.5–6.5 cm broad, with a short [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] and a serrate or doubly serrate margin. At the end of autumn, the green leaves turn yellow, red or crimson.<ref name ="Prunus"/>

The [[flower]]s are produced in clusters of two to five together at nodes on short spurs in spring at the same time as the new leaves appear; they are white to pink, with five petals in the wild type tree. Its [[fruit]], the {{transliteration|ja|sakuranbo}}, has differences from the ''[[Prunus avium]]'' in that sakuranbo are smaller in size and more bitter in taste; the sakuranbo is a [[globose]] black [[drupe]] 8–10{{nbsp}}mm in diameter.  Owing to their bitter taste, the raw sakuranbo is unpalatable and rarely eaten; instead, the seed inside is removed and the fleshy part preserved.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

Because of its evolution, the fruit developed merely as a small, ovoid cherry-like fruit, but it doesn't develop past a small amount of fleshy mass around the seed; as ''P. serrulata'' was bred for its flowers, its fruits do not enlarge the way cherry varieties bred for their fruit do.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

==Cultivars==
{{Main|Cherry blossom}}
Among the ''Prunus serrulata'', many [[cultivars]] derived from Japanese endemic [[Prunus speciosa|''Prunus speciosa'' (Oshima cherry)]], are widely grown as a flowering [[ornamental tree]], both in Japan and throughout the temperate regions of the world. Numerous cultivars have been selected, many of them with double flowers with the [[stamen]]s replaced by additional petals.
According to an unprecedented and detailed DNA study conducted by the Forestry and Forest Products Research Institute in 2014, many of the cherry blossom cultivars used for [[hanami]] around the world were derived from the complicated hybridization of wild species such as ''[[Prunus sargentii|P. sargentii]]'', ''[[Prunus itosakura|P. itosakura]]'', ''[[Prunus leveilleana|P. leveilleana]]'', ''[[Prunus apetala|P. apetala]]'', ''[[Prunus incisa|P. incisa]]'' and ''[[Prunus campanulata|P. campanulata]]'' with the Oshima cherry, an endemic species of Japan.<ref name = "katsuki201586">Toshio Katsuki (2015). ''Sakura'' pp.86-95. [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref><ref name ="ojfc"/>

As the population increased in the southern [[Kanto region]] during the [[Kamakura period]], Oshima cherries, which were originally from [[Izu Oshima]] Island, were brought into [[Honshu]] (the main island of Japan) to be cultivated and brought to [[Kyoto]], the capital of Japan. In the [[Muromachi period]], Oshima cherries were crossed with ''P. yamasakura'', and cultivars of Sato-zakura group such as 'Fugenzo' and 'Mikurumakaishi' began to appear. In the [[Edo period]], various double-flowered cultivars were produced and planted on the banks of rivers, on Buddhist temples, in [[Shinto shrines]] and in [[daimyo]] gardens in urban areas such as [[Edo]], and the common people living in urban areas could enjoy them. In the documents at that time, more than 200 cultivars of cherry trees were recorded, and currently known cultivars of cherry trees such as [[Prunus 'Kanzan'|'Kanzan']] are also mentioned.<ref name = "katsuki201586"/><ref name ="ojfc"/>

In American classification, these cultivars are classified as '''''Prunus serrulata'' var. ''lannesiana''''' or '''''Prunus serrulata'' var. ''pendula'''''  (syn. '''''Prunus lannesiana'''''). However, detailed DNA studies revealed that they were complex interspecific hybrids with the Oshima cherry, so they are classified as the '''''Prunus'' Sato-zakura group''' or '''''Cerasus'' Sato-zakura group'''.<ref name ="katsuki2015137"/><ref name="katsuki201586"/><ref name ="ojfc"/>

'Kanzan' is the most popular Japanese cherry tree cultivar for cherry blossom viewing in Europe and North America. Compared with [[Prunus × yedoensis|'Yoshino cherry']], a representative Japanese cultivar, it is popular because it grows well even in cold regions, is small and easy to plant in the garden, and has large flowers and deep pink petals. In the city of [[Bonn, Germany]], there is a row of cherry trees where 300 kanzan trees were planted in the late 1980s. In Western countries, 'Pink Perfection' and 'Royal Burgundy' originated in 'Kanzan' have been created.<ref name ="katsuki201840">Toshio Katsuki. (2018) ''Sakura no Kagaku (Science of Cherry Blossoms)''. pp.40-42 SB Creative. {{ISBN|978-4797389319}}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20210117034901/https://www.bonn.de/bonn-erleben/besichtigen-entdecken/kirschbluete.php Kirschblüte.] Bundesstadt Bonn.</ref>

In some cultivars, the [[pistil]] changes like a leaf and loses its fertility, and for example, [[:ja:フゲンゾウ|'Fugenzo']] and [[:ja:イチヨウ|'Ichiyo']], can only be propagated by artificial methods such as [[grafting]] and [[cutting]].<ref name ="katsuki2015107">Toshio Katsuki. (2015) ''Sakura'' p.107 [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref>

In cultivation in Europe and North America, it is usually grafted on to ''[[Prunus avium]]'' roots; the cultivated forms rarely bear fruit. It is viewed as part of the Japanese custom of [[Hanami]].{{cn|date=December 2023}}

Some important [[cultivars]] include:
* [[Prunus 'Kanzan'|'Kanzan']]. = 'Sekiyama' or 'Kwanzan'. ''Cerasus'' Sato-zakura Group 'Sekiyama' Koidz<ref name ="katsuki2017">[https://web.archive.org/web/20210301110856/https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/treeforesthealth/21/2/21_93/_pdf Classification and Morphological Identification of Cherry Blossoms.] Toshio Katsuki (2017).</ref>
::Flowers pink, double; young leaves bronze-coloured at first, becoming green.<ref name=POTM2005/><ref>{{cite web |title=''Prunus'' 'Kanzan' AGM |work=Plant Selector |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=1539 |access-date=30 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130517134130/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=1539 |archive-date=17 May 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=''Prunus'' 'Kanzan' |publisher= Missouri Botanic Garden |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=c128 |access-date=30 March 2018}}
</ref> [[List of Award of Garden Merit flowering cherries|Award of Garden Merit]].
* 'Amanogawa'.
::Fastigiate cherry, with columnar habit; flowers semi-double, pale pink.<ref name=POTM2005/>  Award of Garden Merit.
[[File:Kenrokuen-kumagai1.jpg|thumb|[[:ja:ケンロクエンクマガイ|'Choshu-hizakura']]]]
* [[:ja:ケンロクエンクマガイ|'Choshu-hizakura']]  Also known as 'Kenrokuen-kumagai'. ''Crasus'' Sato-zakura Group 'Choshu-hizakura'<ref>[http://db.ffpri.affrc.go.jp/sakura/report.php?recid=1714 Sakura Datebase.] Forestry and Forest Products Research Institute.</ref>
::Large flowers and red leaves open at the same time. In a DNA study published in 2014, 'Choshu-hizakura' and 'Kenrokuen-magai' were found to be the same clone.<ref name ="ojfc"/><ref name ="ojfcffrri"/>
* [[:ja:フゲンゾウ|'Fugenzo']]. = 'Shiro-fugen'. ''Cerasus'' Sato-zakura Group 'Albo-rosea' Makino<ref name ="katsuki2017"/>
::Flowers double, deep pink at first, fading to pale pink. In Japanese, ''fugen'' refers to [[Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]] and ''zo'' refers to an elephant, and the origin of the name comes from the fact that the two [[pistil]]s, which look like leaves, were likened to the tusks of a white elephant on which Samantabhadra rides.<ref name=POTM2005/><ref>{{cite web |title=''Prunus'' 'Shirofugen' |work=Plant Selector |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/89980/i-Prunus-i-Shirofugen/Details |access-date=30 March 2018}}</ref><ref name ="katsuki2015107"/> Award of Garden Merit.
* 'Kiku-shidare'.
::Cheal's Weeping Cherry. Stems weeping; flowers double, pink. Tends to be short-lived.<ref name=POTM2005/>
[[File:イチヨウ全体.jpg|thumb|[[:ja:イチヨウ|'Ichiyo']]]]
* [[:ja:イチヨウ|'Ichiyo']]. ''Cerasus'' Sato-zakura Group 'Hisakura' Koehne<ref name ="katsuki2017"/>
::Flowers double, pale pink at first, fading to white. The name comes from the fact that only one pistil is changed like a leaf, and ''ichi (一)'' means 'one' and ''yo (葉)'' means' leaf'. In the Japanese climate, it is one of the cultivars that are likely to become the largest tree among the double-flowered cherry trees derived from Oshima cherry.<ref name ="katsuki2015107"/> Award of Garden Merit.
* [[:ja:シロタエ|'Shirotae']]. Mt. Fuji Cherry. ''Crasus'' Sato-zakura Group 'Shirotae' Koidz<ref name ="katsuki2017"/>
::Very low, broad crown with nearly horizontal branching; flowers pure white, semi-double.<ref name=POTM2005/><ref>{{cite web |title=''Prunus'' 'Shirotae' |publisher= Missouri Botanic Garden |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=c671 |access-date=30 March 2018}}</ref> Award of Garden Merit.
* [[:ja:タイハク|'Taihaku']]. ''Cerasus'' Sato-zakura Group 'Taihaku' Ingram<ref name ="katsuki2017"/>
::Great White Cherry. Flowers single, white, very large (up to 8 cm diameter); young leaves bronze-coloured at first, becoming green.<ref name=POTM2005/> By the beginning of the 20th century it had already ceased to exist in Japan, but [[Collingwood Ingram]], an English man who had imported it from Japan before then, sent  it back to Japan in 1932.<ref name ="katsuki2015119">Toshio Katsuki. (2015) ''Sakura''. pp.119-123 [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref> Award of Garden Merit.
* [[:ja:ウコン (サクラ)|'Ukon']]. = 'Grandiflora', ''P. serrulata'' f. ''grandiflora'' Wagner. ''Cerasus'' Sato-zakura Group 'Grandiflora' A. Wagner<ref name ="katsuki2017"/>
::Green cerry Cherry. Flowers semi-double, cream-white or pale yellow. Young leaves light bronzy-green. Fall leaf color can be purple or rusty-red.<ref name=POTM2005/><ref>{{cite web |title=''Prunus'' 'Ukon' AGM |work=Plant Selector |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/66900/i-Prunus-i-Ukon/Details |access-date=30 March 2018}}</ref> 'Ukon' was developed in the Edo period.<ref name ="katsuki20158695">Toshio Katsuki. (2015) ''Sakura''. pp.86-95 p.104 [[Iwanami Shoten]]. {{ISBN|978-4004315346}}</ref> Award of Garden Merit.
